(5519.) According to Andronicus, the year
of the Greeks.
After Tiberius Caesar, Gaius Caesar [reigned] four years.
Agrippa, who was named Herod:
he was the son of Aristobulus, the son of Herod the slayer of the infants, by Mariamne the daughter of Hyrcanus the high priest.
When in the days of Tiberius he went up to Rome to accuse Herod the tetrarch,
who is Antipas,
he was imprisoned there.
And while he was imprisoned,
he prayed that Gaius would become king.
Therefore, when he became king,
he gave him the tetrarchies of Philip and of Lysanias.
And because of this, Herodias reproached Herod Antipas (Antipater?):
"Because you did not go to Caesar, you were deprived of the rule.
For if Agrippa, from being an ordinary citizen, became a ruler,
how much more you, [being already] from the tetrarchy!"
And because of this, when he went up to Rome to obtain royalty,
Gaius became angry and cast him into exile together with his wife,
and there they died.
And in the first year that this Agrippa reigned, he killed James,
not the brother of our Lord,
(but the son of Zebedee), whom Paul mentions,
and he was crowned by a fuller's club,
and not by the sword of Agrippa.
And at that time, Felix was sent [as] prefect of Egypt,
and he oppressed the Jews for seven years.
And because of this, ambassadors were sent to Gaius to appease him:
Josephus the sage, and Philo the Hebrew philosopher from Alexandria.
And in the fourth year of Gaius, he commanded Petronius, the prefect of Syria,
to set up his statues in the Temple and in the synagogues of the Jews.
And that [saying] of Daniel was fulfilled concerning the unclean sign standing in the holy place.
And when Agrippa had completed three years of his reign,
he came to Caesarea and held a festival of spectacles on behalf of Caesar's life.
And on the second day of the spectacles,
he put on a robe woven with silver,
and came in the morning to the theater.
